claim: Natural rubber (NR) is stored in latex as rubber particles (RPs), which are rubber molecules surrounded by a lipid monolayer.
source: Natural rubber (NR) is stored in latex as rubber particles (RPs), rubber molecules surrounded by a lipid monolayer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about rubber particle structure.

claim: Rubber transferase (RTase) is believed to be a member of the cis-prenyltransferase (cPT) family.
source: Rubber transferase (RTase), the enzyme responsible for NR biosynthesis, is believed to be a member of the cis-prenyltransferase (cPT) family.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a belief based on prior research.

claim: None of the recombinant cPTs have shown RTase activity independently.
source: However, none of the recombinant cPTs have shown RTase activity independently.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the literature review in the introduction.

claim: HRT1 exhibits distinct RTase activity in vitro only when introduced on detergent-washed Hevea RPs (WRPs) by a cell-free translation-coupled system.
source: We show that HRT1, a cPT from Heveabrasiliensis, exhibits distinct RTase activity in vitro only when it is introduced on detergent-washed HeveaRPs (WRPs) by a cell-free translation-coupled system.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A heterologous cPT from Lactuca sativa exhibited RTase activity when introduced on Hevea RPs.
source: Using this system, a heterologous cPT from Lactucasativa also exhibited RTase activity, indicating proper introduction of cPT on RP is the key to reconstitute active RTase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 10.

claim: Proper introduction of cPT on RP is the key to reconstitute active RTase.
source: Using this system, a heterologous cPT from Lactucasativa also exhibited RTase activity, indicating proper introduction of cPT on RP is the key to reconstitute active RTase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with both HRT1 and LsCPT3.

claim: A protein complex consisting of HRT1, rubber elongation factor (REF), and HRT1-REF BRIDGING PROTEIN (HRBP) forms on rubber particles.
source: RP proteomics and interaction network analyses revealed the formation of the protein complex consisting of HRT1, rubber elongation factor (REF) and HRT1-REF BRIDGING PROTEIN.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data (Figure 2), Y2H assays (Figure 3), BiFC assays (Figure 4), and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 6).

claim: The HRT1-containing complex functions as the NR biosynthetic machinery.
source: The RTase activity enhancement observed for the complex assembled on WRPs indicates the HRT1-containing complex functions as the NR biosynthetic machinery.
evidence: This is supported by the RTase activity assays showing enhanced activity with the three-component system (Figure 9A).

claim: More than 2500 plant species are known to biosynthesize NR.
source: Although more than 2500 plant species are known to biosynthesize NR (Metcalfe, 1967; van Beilen and Poirier, 2007), industrial production of NR depends solely on latex, the cytoplasm of highly specialized cells known as laticifers harvested from the Para rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Industrial production of NR depends solely on latex from Hevea brasiliensis.
source: Although more than 2500 plant species are known to biosynthesize NR (Metcalfe, 1967; van Beilen and Poirier, 2007), industrial production of NR depends solely on latex, the cytoplasm of highly specialized cells known as laticifers harvested from the Para rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on cited literature.

claim: RPs primarily consist of a hydrophobic rubber core enclosed by a lipid monolayer.
source: NR exists in latex as rubber particles (RPs), which primarily consist of a hydrophobic rubber core enclosed by a lipid monolayer (Cornish et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: RTase was reported to be the enzyme responsible for NR biosynthesis from RPs in the 1960s.
source: In the 1960s, the enzyme responsible for NR biosynthesis from RPs was reported to be rubber transferase (RTase) [EC.2.5.1.20] (Archer, 1969), although its proteinaceous components and catalytic mechanism were not elucidated.
evidence: This is cited from historical literature.

claim: The backbone structure of NR comprises cis-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus.
source: The backbone structure of NR comprises of a cis-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus (Tanaka et al., 1996; Eng et al., 1994) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is cited from literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The basic backbone structures of cis,trans-mixed polyisoprenoid alcohols are biosynthesized via sequential cis-condensation of IPP onto all-trans short-chain prenyl diphosphates.
source: Generally, the basic backbone structures of cis,trans-mixed polyisoprenoid alcohols, polyprenols and dolichols (C30–C120), are biosynthesized via sequential cis-condensation of the C5 isoprene unit, isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP), onto all-trans short-chain prenyl diphosphates such as geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10) E,E-farnesyl diphosphate (FPP, C15), and E,E,E-geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP, C20).
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about polyisoprenoid biosynthesis.

claim: cis-Prenyltransferase (cPT) catalyzes the sequential cis-condensation reaction to form polyisoprenoid alcohols.
source: This reaction is catalyzed by cis-prenyltransferase (cPT) (Takahashi and Koyama, 2006; Koyama, 1999) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is cited from literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The NR carbon chain length (C>1500) is much longer than that of other cis,trans-mixed polyisoprenoid alcohols such as dolichols.
source: The common structural unit of polyisoprenoid alcohols and NR suggests that RTase is a member of the cPT family, although the NR carbon chain length (C>1500) is much longer than that of other cis,trans-mixed polyisoprenoid alcohols, such as dolichols which are indispensable as sugar carrier lipids during the protein glycosylations in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Helenius and Aebi, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between NR and other polyisoprenoid alcohols.

claim: HRT1 and HRT2 are two cPT homologues isolated from H. brasiliensis that are predominantly expressed in latex.
source: We previously isolated two cPT homologues, designated HRT1 and HRT2, from H. brasiliensis, which are predominantly expressed in latex (Asawatreratanakul et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Recombinant proteins of HRT1 and HRT2 expressed in E. coli did not exhibit distinct cPT activity independently in vitro.
source: Recombinant proteins of HRT1 and HRT2 expressed in Escherichia coli did not exhibit distinct cPT activity independently in vitro.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Recombinant proteins of HRT1 and HRT2 expressed in yeast and Arabidopsis showed significant activity, producing C80–100 polyisoprenoids, but failed to produce longer chain products corresponding to NR.
source: While the recombinant proteins of HRT1 and HRT2, expressed in yeast and Arabidopsis showed significant activity, producing C80–100 polyisoprenoids, they failed to produce longer chain products corresponding to NR (Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: cPT homologues have been isolated from latex of Russian dandelion, lettuce, and Euphorbia characias, but their recombinant proteins show no RTase activity in vitro.
source: Recently, cPT homologues expressed in latex of other NR-producing plants, such as Russian dandelion (Taraxacum koksaghyz) (Schmidt et al., 2010a; Schmidt et al., 2010b), lettuce (Lactuca sativa) (Qu et al., 2015) and Euphorbia characias (Spanò et al., 2015), have been isolated, although their recombinant proteins show no RTase activity in vitro.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: RNA interference-mediated knock-down of cPTs expressed in the latex of Taraxacum brevicorniculatum decreased latex rubber content.
source: RNA interference-mediated knock-down of cPTs expressed in the latex of Taraxacum brevicorniculatum have been shown to decrease latex rubber content (Post et al., 2012), suggesting the involvement of cPT in NR formation.
evidence: This is cited from literature and suggests involvement of cPT in NR formation.

claim: There is no direct evidence to date suggesting that the cPTs expressed in latex are RTases.
source: However, there is no direct evidence to date suggesting that the cPTs expressed in latex are RTases.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Latex-specific cPTs are thought to require eukaryotic cell-specific factor(s) to exhibit cPT activity and additional factor(s) in the latex to modify these cPTs into RTases.
source: Therefore, latex-specific cPTs are thought to require eukaryotic cell-specific factor(s) to exhibit cPT activity and additional factor(s) in the latex to modify these cPTs into RTases.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on previous observations.

claim: NgBR from humans contains three predicted transmembrane domains in its N-terminal region and a domain exhibiting low similarity to cPT in the C-terminal half.
source: NgBR from humans, originally identified as a receptor for the N-terminal portion of reticulon 4B/Nogo-B (Miao et al., 2006), contains three predicted transmembrane domains in its N-terminal region, and a domain exhibiting low similarity to cPT in the C-terminal half, although it does not have catalytic residues conserved among cPTs.
evidence: This is cited from literature describing the structure of human NgBR.

claim: NgBR can interact with human cPT HDS/hCIT to stabilize it on the ER membrane, resulting in cPT activity enhancement.
source: In the cPT-like domain, NgBR can also interact with a human cPT HDS/hCIT (Shridas et al., 2003; Endo et al., 2003) to stabilize it on the ER membrane, resulting in cPT activity enhancement (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Knock-down or mutation of NgBR causes defects in protein N-glycosylation as a consequence of a reduction in the level of dolichyl phosphates and dolichol-linked oligosaccharides.
source: Knock-down (Harrison et al., 2011) or a mutation (Eng et al., 1994) of NgBR causes defects in protein N-glycosylation as a consequence of a reduction in the level of dolichyl phosphates and dolichol-linked oligosaccharides, indicating that NgBR is an HDS-interacting protein and this interaction is critical for its activity.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: NUS1, a yeast homolog of NgBR, is implicated to have an important role in N-glycosylation and cPT activity.
source: NUS1, a yeast homolog of NgBR, is implicated to have an important role in N-glycosylation and cPT activity (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: A defect in LEW1, a counterpart of NgBR in Arabidopsis thaliana, results in reduced levels of dolichol contents and protein glycosylation.
source: It has also been reported that a defect in LEW1, a counterpart of NgBR in Arabidopsis thaliana, results in reduced levels of dolichol contents and protein glycosylation (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Various eukaryotic cPTs heterologously expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have shown distinct activity without co-expression of their partner NgBR family protein.
source: Moreover, its role as an essential subunit of a deduced cPT-containing protein complex is controversial as various eukaryotic cPTs heterologously expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have shown distinct activity without co-expression of their partner NgBR family protein (Asawatreratanakul et al., 2003; Takahashi et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2010b; Shridas et al., 2003; Endo et al., 2003; Harrison et al., 2011; Cunillera et al., 2000; Akhtar et al., 2013; Kera et al., 2012; Surmacz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from multiple literature sources.

claim: CHAPS was the best detergent for removing protein from the RPs and had a relatively low inhibitory effect on the RTase activity among the 15 detergents tested.
source: Before the proteomic analyses, proteins unnecessary for RTase activity were removed from RPs by washing with CHAPS as it was the best detergent for removing protein from the RPs and had a relatively low inhibitory effect on the RTase activity among the 15 detergents tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stepwise washing with buffers containing CHAPS resulted in washing-out a lot of the RP proteins, whereas 80% of the RTase activity was retained on the detergent-washed RPs.
source: Stepwise washing with buffers containing CHAPS resulted in washing-out a lot of the RP proteins (Figure 2A), whereas 80% of the RTase activity was retained on the detergent-washed RPs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Peptides corresponding to HRT1 or HRT2 were identified among 137 proteins (115 subfamilies) assigned in the proteome analyses of detergent-washed RPs.
source: Peptides corresponding to HRT1 or HRT2 were identified among 137 proteins (115 subfamilies) assigned (Figure 2—source data 1,2); however, this result does not allow to discriminate between these two cPTs since some detected fragments correspond to the sequences shared by both enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: No other prenyltransferase or enzyme in the IPP biosynthetic pathways was detected from the proteome analyses of the detergent-washed RPs.
source: No other prenyltransferase or enzyme in the IPP biosynthetic pathways was detected from the proteome analyses of the detergent-washed RPs, in contrast with previous proteome analyses of non-detergent-washed RPs from H. brasiliensis, in which several homologues of cPT (Dai et al., 2013) and a homologue of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (Xiang et al., 2012), one of late-limiting enzyme in the IPP biosynthetic pathway, were detected.
evidence: This is a result from the proteomics analysis, contrasted with previous studies.

claim: A protein assigned as a homologous protein of NgBR was identified in the proteome analyses of detergent-washed RPs.
source: However, we also identified a protein assigned as a homologous protein of NgBR (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a result from the proteomics analysis.

claim: The NgBR homologue from H. brasiliensis showed greater similarity to higher plant orthologues that have one predicted transmembrane domain in the N-terminal region.
source: The NgBR homologue from H. brasiliensis showed greater similarity to higher plant orthologues (Figure 2C) that have one predicted transmembrane domain in the N-terminal region (Qu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2008; Brasher et al., 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2C) and sequence comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: The NgBR homologue is predominantly expressed in latex.
source: Quantitative analyses of the transcript levels in various tissues showed predominant expression of the NgBR homologue in latex (Figure 2D), along with cPTs (HRT1 and HRT2) and REF (Aoki et al., 2014a), and the transcript level of the NgBR homologue in latex was comparable to those of HRT1 and HRT2, but 540-fold lower than that of REF (Aoki et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The transcript level of the NgBR homologue in latex was comparable to those of HRT1 and HRT2, but 540-fold lower than that of REF.
source: Quantitative analyses of the transcript levels in various tissues showed predominant expression of the NgBR homologue in latex (Figure 2D), along with cPTs (HRT1 and HRT2) and REF (Aoki et al., 2014a), and the transcript level of the NgBR homologue in latex was comparable to those of HRT1 and HRT2, but 540-fold lower than that of REF (Aoki et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data and cited from previous work.

claim: The NgBR homologue might possibly form a complex with HRT1/HRT2 and REF on RPs.
source: These results suggested that the NgBR homologue might possibly form a complex with HRT1/HRT2 and REF on RPs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the proteomics and expression data.

claim: HRBP can interact with HRT1 and REF, but not with HRT2, according to split-ubiquitin-based Y2H assays.
source: The assays showed that the NgBR homologue could interact with HRT1 and REF, but not with HRT2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The NgBR homologue was named HRT1-REF bridging protein (HRBP).
source: We therefore named the NgBR homologue HRT1-REF bridging protein (HRBP).
evidence: This is stated as a naming decision based on the interaction data.

claim: Y2H analyses indicated distinct REF–REF, HRBP–HRBP and REF–SRPP interactions.
source: The Y2H analyses also indicated distinct REF–REF, HRBP–HRBP and REF–SRPP interactions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neither homodimeric nor heterodimeric interactions for HRT1 and HRT2 were detected in Y2H assays.
source: Neither homodimeric nor heterodimeric interactions for HRT1 and HRT2 were detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in contrast with bacterial cPTs which function as homodimers (Fujihashi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BiFC assays in Nicotiana benthamiana leaf epidermal cells revealed that the interaction partnerships detected by Y2H were also detected in planta.
source: A bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assay with split mVenus protein fragments in Nicotiana benthamiana leaf epidermal cells revealed that these interaction partnerships were also detected in planta, almost independent of orientations of the mVenus fragments fused in-frame with target proteins (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: BiFC signals indicating an HRT1–HRBP interaction were observed at the Golgi.
source: BiFC signals indicating an HRT1–HRBP interaction were observed at the Golgi, harboring or surrounding fluorescence signals for a mTurquoise2 (mTq2)-fused marker protein (XT-Golgi-mTq2), which accumulates exclusively in a medial subset of the cisternae of Golgi stacks (Pagny et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HRBP–REF interactions were observed on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles, and did not overlap with the Golgi signals.
source: HRBP–REF interactions were observed on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles, and did not overlap with the Golgi signals, and REF–REF interactions were localized mainly on oval bodies and smaller spherical particles.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: REF–REF interactions were localized mainly on oval bodies and smaller spherical particles.
source: HRBP–REF interactions were observed on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles, and did not overlap with the Golgi signals, and REF–REF interactions were localized mainly on oval bodies and smaller spherical particles.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HRBP–HRBP interactions were only observed at the perimeters of spherical particles.
source: HRBP–HRBP interactions were only observed at the perimeters of spherical particles.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Distinct fluorescent signals indicating an HRT2–HRBP interaction were observed at the plasma membrane in the BiFC assay.
source: In contrast to the result obtained by the Y2H assay, distinct fluorescent signals indicating an HRT2–HRBP interaction were observed at the plasma membrane in the BiFC assay.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HRBP and REF are predominantly localized at the ER.
source: The fluorescence signals for mTq2-fused HRBP or REF showed network-like patterns, which almost overlapped with an mCherry (mChe)-HDEL ER marker (Nelson et al., 2007) (Figure 5A), indicating that these proteins were predominantly localized at the ER.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HRT1 is stabilized in N. benthamiana cells by complex formation with HRBP, which induces translocation of HRBP from the ER to the Golgi.
source: These results indicate that HRT1 is stabilized in N. benthamiana cells by complex formation with the HRBP, which induces translocation of HRBP from the ER to the Golgi.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HRT2 is stabilized by HRBP in N. benthamiana cells and localizes at the plasma membrane.
source: In the co-expression system of HRT2:mTq2 and HRBP:mVenus, HRT2:mTq2-derived signals localized at the plasma membrane, showing a partial overlap with a marker protein mChe-AtPIP2A localized at the ER to the plasma membrane (Nelson et al., 2007). These results indicate that HRT2 is also stabilized by HRBP in N. benthamiana cells.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Subcellular localization of HRBP:mVenus was clearly altered from the ER to the plasma membrane when co-expressed with HRT2:mTq2.
source: Surprisingly, in this co-expression system, subcellular localization of HRBP:mVenus was clearly altered from the ER to the plasma membrane (Figure 5A), concordant with the BiFC signals for the HRT2–HRBP interaction at the plasma membrane (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The different subcellular localization of HRT1 and HRT2 co-expressed with HRBP indicates that they have different roles.
source: Taken together with the basic subcellular localization of HRBP on the ER, HRBP is assumed to assist incorporation or stabilization of HRT2 on the ER membrane and to be co-translocated to the plasma membrane with HRT2. Additionally, the different subcellular localization of HRT1 and HRT2 co-expressed with HRBP indicates that they have different roles.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data.

claim: HRT1 may be more important in NR biosynthesis than HRT2.
source: Considering that RPs are speculated to originate from the ER or Golgi apparatus (Chrispeels and Herman, 2000), HRT1 may be more important in NR biosynthesis than HRT2.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data and cited knowledge about RP origin.

claim: The subcellular localizations of REF and HRBP were not influenced by co-expression.
source: By contrast, the subcellular localizations of REF and HRBP were not influenced by co-expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: When REF:mCherry was co-expressed, BiFC signals for the HRT1-HRBP interaction were not observed at the Golgi, but overlapped with the network-like REF:mCherry signals.
source: When REF:mCherry was co-expressed, BiFC signals for the HRT1-HRBP interaction were not observed at the Golgi, but overlapped with the network-like REF:mCherry signals (Figure 4B), indicating REF-oriented translocation of the HRT1-HRBP complex to the ER.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: REF-oriented translocation of the HRT1-HRBP complex to the ER occurs when REF is co-expressed.
source: When REF:mCherry was co-expressed, BiFC signals for the HRT1-HRBP interaction were not observed at the Golgi, but overlapped with the network-like REF:mCherry signals (Figure 4B), indicating REF-oriented translocation of the HRT1-HRBP complex to the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the BiFC assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Weak BiFC signals indicating an HRT1-REF interaction were observed on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles when HRBP without fluorescent tag was co-introduced.
source: As expected from the Y2H assay results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we could not detect a distinct BiFC signal indicating an HRT1-REF interaction, but could observe weak BiFC signals on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles when HRBP without fluorescent tag was co-introduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting an HRBP-mediated interaction between HRT1 and REF.
evidence: This is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: HRBP mediates the interaction between HRT1 and REF.
source: As expected from the Y2H assay results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we could not detect a distinct BiFC signal indicating an HRT1-REF interaction, but could observe weak BiFC signals on aggregates of spherical bodies and smaller independent particles when HRBP without fluorescent tag was co-introduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting an HRBP-mediated interaction between HRT1 and REF.
evidence: This is inferred from the BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Co-expression of three proteins, HRT1:mTq2, HRBP:mVenus and REF:mCherry, revealed that the fluorescent signals for each protein were almost overlapped, showing network-like patterns.
source: Co-expression of three proteins, HRT1:mTq2, HRBP:mVenus and REF:mCherry, revealed that the fluorescent signals for each protein were almost overlapped, showing network-like patterns (Figure 5B), contrasting with the fluorescent signals on the Golgi and small spherical bodies in the cells co-expressing HRT1:mTq2 and HRBP:mVenus (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The plasma membrane localizations of HRT2:mTq2 and HRBP:mVenus were not influenced by the co-expression of REF:mCherry localized at the ER.
source: On the other hands, the plasma membrane localizations of HRT2:mTq2 and HRBP:mVenus were not influenced by the co-expression of REF:mCherry localized at the ER (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A protein complex consisting of HRT1, HRBP and REF is primarily localized on the ER and ER-emerged-specific particles.
source: Taken together, these results indicated formation of a protein complex consisting of HRT1, HRBP and REF primarily localized on the ER and ER-emerged-specific particles.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data.

claim: HRT1/HRT2 and REF were co-immunoprecipitated with HRBP from solubilized RP-bound proteins.
source: As expected from the interaction partnerships revealed by Y2H and BiFC analyses, HRT1/HRT2 and REF were co-immunoprecipitated with HRBP (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HRBP and REF were co-precipitated with HRT1/HRT2 when anti-HRT1/HRT2 antibody was utilized for immunoprecipitation.
source: Moreover, when anti-HRT1/HRT2 antibody was utilized for immunoprecipitation, not only HRBP, but also REF was co-precipitated with HRT1/HRT2.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The ternary protein complexes (HRT1/HRT2-HRBP-REF) form on RPs in vivo.
source: The results suggested the formations of the ternary protein complexes (HRT1/HRT2-HRBP-REF) on RPs in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: No RTase activity was detected from any proteoliposomes with expressed HRT1, HRBP, and REF.
source: Most of the expressed HRT1 was incorporated into liposomes regardless of the co-existence of HRBP and REF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). However, no RTase activity was detected from any proteoliposomes (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from the proteoliposome experiments.

claim: Washing 50kRPs with 8 mM CHAPS for 1 hr resulted in removal of a lot of RP proteins, including REF and SRPP, whereas 89% of the RTase activity was retained on the WRPs.
source: Washing in this condition resulted in removal of a lot of RP proteins, including REF and SRPP (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), whereas 89% of the RTase activity was retained on the WRPs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most expressed proteins tested were incorporated into WRPs.
source: Similar to the case of proteoliposomes, most expressed proteins tested were incorporated into WRPs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: HRBP and REF promote the incorporation of HRT1 into WRPs, but are not necessary for anchoring HRT1 on WRPs.
source: When these target proteins were expressed alone, some HRT1 proteins existed in the soluble fraction, whereas HRBP and REF were incorporated almost completely into WRP. However, the amount of HRT1 not incorporated on WRPs was decreased by co-expression of HRBP and REF, indicating that these proteins promotes the incorporation of HRT1 into WRPs, but are not necessary for anchoring HRT1 on WRPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Detergent washing induced RP coagulation and increased the apparent average diameter from 222 nm to 1244 nm.
source: Detergent washing induced RP coagulation and increased the apparent average diameter; the average diameter of RPs before the detergent treatment was 222 nm whereas that of WRPs was 1244 nm (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 8.

claim: REF expression resulted in decreased WRP coagulation, lowering the apparent average diameter towards that of the non-detergent-washed RPs.
source: Interestingly, however, REF expression resulted in decreased WRP coagulation, lowering the apparent average diameter towards that of the non-detergent-washed RPs, indicating that REF stabilizes WRP by preventing aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 8.

claim: REF stabilizes WRP by preventing aggregation.
source: Interestingly, however, REF expression resulted in decreased WRP coagulation, lowering the apparent average diameter towards that of the non-detergent-washed RPs, indicating that REF stabilizes WRP by preventing aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Coagulation of WRPs was inhibited when three proteins, HRT1, HRBP and REF, were co-expressed.
source: This effect was dominant for the coagulation-inducible proteins, HRBP and HRT1; coagulation of WRPs was inhibited when three proteins, HRT1, HRBP and REF, were co-expressed.
evidence: This is supported by dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The introduction of HRT1 onto WRPs distinctly increased the RTase activity.
source: The RTase assay for the exogenous protein-introduced WRPs by using 14C-IPP and FPP as substrates revealed that the introduction of HRT1 onto WRPs distinctly increased the RTase activity (Figure 9A), whereas HRBP or REF alone did not activate the background activity of WRPs (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The HRT1-derived RTase activity was enhanced by co-expression of HRBP and was markedly activated by additional introduction of REF.
source: The HRT1-derived RTase activity was enhanced by co-expression of HRBP and was markedly activated by additional introduction of REF.
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 14C-IPP incorporation in the assays of WRPs carrying three proteins was increasing linearly during 20 hr of the reaction time.
source: 14C-IPP incorporation in the assays of WRPs carrying three proteins was increasing linearly during 20 hr of the reaction time, whereas for WRPs carrying HRT1 only or two proteins, HRT1 and HRBP, the incorporation was weakened after 8 hr, suggesting that co-expression of REF and HRBP stabilized HRT1 on WRPs.
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Co-expression of REF and HRBP stabilized HRT1 on WRPs.
source: 14C-IPP incorporation in the assays of WRPs carrying three proteins was increasing linearly during 20 hr of the reaction time, whereas for WRPs carrying HRT1 only or two proteins, HRT1 and HRBP, the incorporation was weakened after 8 hr, suggesting that co-expression of REF and HRBP stabilized HRT1 on WRPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The RTase activity of WRPs carrying three proteins depended on the HRT1 and HRBP protein levels, and the activity reached a plateau when the HRT1 and HRBP levels were apparently equivalent.
source: The RTase activity of WRPs carrying three proteins depended on the HRT1 and HRBP protein levels, and the activity reached a plateau when the HRT1 and HRBP levels were apparently equivalent (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The RTase activity of the triple components showed a strict allylic substrate dependency; the RTase was most active with FPP (C15).
source: The RTase activity of the triple components showed a strict allylic substrate dependency; the RTase was most active with FPP (C15) while the activity was low in the absence of an allylic substrate (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: GPP and GGPP showed 83% and 93% activities, respectively, compared to FPP when the triple components were used for the reactions.
source: Other allylic substrates showed comparable activities when the triple components were used for the reactions (e.g., GPP and GGPP showed 83% and 93% activities, respectively), and the patterns of allylic substrate dependency were quite similar to those of the control reactions using WRPs expressing REF only (Figure 9C) and WRPs alone as reported elsewhere (Rojruthai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The size distributions of polyisoprenoids synthesized in vitro with WRPs carrying HRT1 were similar to those with control WRPs, showing unimodal size distributions with a peak at >106 as endogenous NR in WRPs.
source: Gel-permeation chromatography (GPC) of the 14C-IPP-derived reaction products revealed that the size distributions of polyisoprenoids synthesized in vitro with WRPs carrying HRT1 were similar to those with control WRPs, showing unimodal size distributions with a peak at >106 as endogenous NR in WRPs (Figure 9D), concordant with previous reports for small rubber particles (Rojruthai et al., 2010) that corresponds to the 50kRP in this study.
evidence: This is supported by GPC data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The size distributions of the HRT1-derived polyisoprenoids were not influenced by co-expression of HRBP and REF.
source: The size distributions of the HRT1-derived polyisoprenoids were not influenced by co-expression of HRBP and REF, suggesting that complex formation on the WRPs does not affect the product chain-length regulation mechanism of HRT1.
evidence: This is supported by GPC data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Complex formation on the WRPs does not affect the product chain-length regulation mechanism of HRT1.
source: The size distributions of the HRT1-derived polyisoprenoids were not influenced by co-expression of HRBP and REF, suggesting that complex formation on the WRPs does not affect the product chain-length regulation mechanism of HRT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the GPC data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: HRT1 on WRP catalyzes a de novo rubber formation using allylic primer substrates, GPP, FPP and GGPP, rather than addition of IPP onto the α-terminus of pre-existing rubber molecules in WRPs.
source: These results, together with the allylic primer requirement for the RTase reaction (Figure 9C), suggest a possibility that HRT1 on WRP catalyzes a de novo rubber formation using allylic primer substrates, GPP, FPP and GGPP, rather than addition of IPP onto the α-terminus of pre-existing rubber molecules in WRPs, which is concordant with the backbone structure of NR, a cis-1,4-polyisoprene with several trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus (Tanaka et al., 1996; Eng et al., 1994).
evidence: This is inferred from the RTase activity assay data and cited structural information about NR.

claim: LsCPT3 showed a comparable level of IPP incorporation activity to HRT1 in the 18-h reactions on WRPs.
source: LsCPT3 showed a comparable level of IPP incorporation activity in the 18-h reactions (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: LsCPTL2 itself showed a slight enhancement of IPP incorporation activity of WRPs.
source: Interestingly, LsCPTL2 itself showed a slight enhancement of IPP incorporation activity of WRPs.
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Co-expression of LsCPTL2 with LsCPT3 resulted in an increase of the activity of LsCPT3.
source: Co-expression of LsCPTL2 with LsCPT3 resulted in an increase of the activity of LsCPT3 (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: GPC analyses of the reaction products from the lettuce cPT on WRPs showed similar distributions of polyisoprenoids from those of HRT1 or HRT1-HRBP co-expression.
source: GPC analyses of the reaction products from the lettuce cPT on WRPs showed similar distributions of polyisoprenoids from those of HRT1 or HRT1-HRBP co-expression (Figure 10B), demonstrating that heterologous cPT reconstituted on the Hevea WRP could also exhibit distinct RTase activity.
evidence: This is supported by GPC data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Heterologous cPT reconstituted on the Hevea WRP could exhibit distinct RTase activity.
source: GPC analyses of the reaction products from the lettuce cPT on WRPs showed similar distributions of polyisoprenoids from those of HRT1 or HRT1-HRBP co-expression (Figure 10B), demonstrating that heterologous cPT reconstituted on the Hevea WRP could also exhibit distinct RTase activity.
evidence: This is supported by GPC data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The key factor for the reconstitution of RTase activity is not an unknown interacting protein for cPT but the proper introduction of cPT on the target membrane architecture of WRPs.
source: These results support our idea that the key factor for the reconstitution of RTase activity is not an unknown interacting protein for cPT but the proper introduction of cPT on the target membrane architecture of WRPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with both HRT1 and LsCPT3.

claim: This study established a novel system for cell-free, translation-coupled, hydrophobic protein introduction on detergent-washed RPs from H. brasiliensis, allowing de novo synthesis of NR in vitro by the recombinant protein.
source: In this study, we established a novel system for cell-free, translation-coupled, hydrophobic protein introduction on detergent-washed RPs from H. brasiliensis, allowing de novo synthesis of NR in vitro by the recombinant protein.
evidence: This is stated as a primary achievement of the study.

claim: The key factor for reconstitution of RTase activity of latex cPTs in vitro is proper arrangement of cPT on the specific architecture of WRPs.
source: Additionally, we demonstrated that the key factor for reconstitution of RTase activity of latex cPTs in vitro is proper arrangement of cPT on the specific architecture of WRPs.
evidence: This is stated as a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Refolded HRT2 expressed in E. coli was significantly activated by the addition of washed-bottom fraction (BF) of H. brasiliensis latex, resulting in the formation of polyisoprenes with similar molecular size distributions as that of the NR in Hevea latex.
source: In a previous study to elucidate activation mechanism of cPT as RTase, we showed that the refolded HRT2, which was heterologously expressed in E. coli and purified from its insoluble membrane fraction under denaturing conditions, was significantly activated by the addition of washed-bottom fraction (BF) of H. brasiliensis latex. This resulted in the formation of polyisoprenes with similar molecular size distributions as that of the NR in Hevea latex (Asawatreratanakul et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Refolded recombinant HRT1 was not activated by the addition of washed-bottom fraction.
source: Whereas the refolded recombinant HRT1 was not activated.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Both HRT2 and HRT1 show distinct cPT activity in the yeast system, producing polyisoprenoids with chain-lengths ranging from C80 to C100.
source: In this yeast system, both HRT2 and HRT1 show distinct cPT activity, producing polyisoprenoids with chain-lengths ranging from C80 to C100 as general eukaryotic long-chain cPTs.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The catalytic properties of HRT1 and HRT2 have never been successfully modified into RTase by the addition of any latex fractions in the yeast system.
source: However, their catalytic properties have never been successfully modified into RTase by the addition of any latex fractions (Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Both HRT1 and HRT2 may require additional factor(s) present within the eukaryotic cell to exhibit cPT activity and other latex-specific factor(s) to exhibit RTase activity.
source: These facts suggest that both, HRT1 and HRT2 may require additional factor(s) present within the eukaryotic cell to exhibit cPT activity and other latex-specific factor(s) to exhibit RTase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous experimental results.

claim: Eukaryotic post-translational modifications such as glycosylations in the ER are unlikely to be key activation factors of eukaryotic cPTs.
source: Eukaryotic post-translational modifications such as glycosylations in the ER were considered to be potential candidates for a key activation factor of eukaryotic cPTs generally localised to the ER (Shridas et al., 2003; Sato et al., 2001). However, this is unlikely since in this study, recombinant HRT1 and LsCPT3 showed distinct RTase activity in vitro (Figures 9 and 10) when they were introduced on RPs by means of the wheat germ cell-free system, in which no post-translational modifications occur without supplementation of donor substrates and cofactors (Harbers, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in this study and cited knowledge about the wheat germ cell-free system.

claim: NgBR homologs on RPs were identified from lettuce and Russian dandelion using an RP proteomics approach.
source: Recently, NgBR homologs on RPs were identified from other NR producing plants, lettuce, and Russian dandelion, using an RP proteomics approach, although no cPT homolog was detected in these proteomics analyses (Qu et al., 2015; Janina, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: NgBR homologs from lettuce and Russian dandelion interact with cPT(s) exclusively expressed in latex.
source: These NgBR homologs were shown to interact with cPT(s) exclusively expressed in latex.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: Knockdown of NgBR homologs in lettuce and Russian dandelion results in significant decrease of rubber content.
source: A knockdown of these NgBR homologs results in significant decrease of rubber content, suggesting involvement of the NgBR homologs in the NR biosynthesis of these NR-producing plants.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: Short- or middle-chain cPTs from Solanum lycopersicum, heterologously expressed in E. coli, exhibit a distinct cPT activity independently in vitro, producing polyisoprenoids shorter than C60.
source: Short- or middle-chain cPTs from Solanum lycopersicum, heterologously expressed in E. coli, exhibit a distinct cPT activity independently in vitro, producing polyisoprenoids shorter than C60 (Akhtar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: The recombinant protein of a cis,trans-mixed heptaprenyl diphosphate (C35) synthase from A. thaliana exhibits a cPT activity independently without corresponding NgBR family protein.
source: Additionally, the recombinant protein of a cis,trans-mixed heptaprenyl diphosphate (C35) synthase from A. thalina, also exhibits a cPT activity independently without corresponding NgBR family protein (Kera et al., 2012; Surmacz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: The NgBR family protein is considered to be a subunit protein of a long-chain cPT on the ER, responsible for the dolichol or NR formations, resulting in enhancement of cPT activity.
source: Taken together, the NgBR family protein is considered to be a subunit protein of a long-chain cPT on the ER, responsible for the dolichol or NR formations, resulting in enhancement of cPT activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature.

claim: An NgBR family protein is not necessary for the catalytic activity of cPT to produce polyisoprenoids that correspond to NR.
source: In vitro results in the present study emphasize that an NgBR family protein is not necessary for the catalytic activity of cPT to produce polyisoprenoids that correspond to NR; HRT1 and LsCPT3 showed a significant rubber-producing activity when introduced into WRPs (Figures 9, 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in this study.

claim: It is unlikely that the small amount of HRBP retained on RPs after the detergent wash could have interacted with LsCPT3 as a surrogate partner for its activation.
source: Due to low amino acid sequence identities between HRT1/HRT2, and LsCPT3 and between HRBP and LsCPTL2 (53% and 45%, respectively), it is unlikely that the small amount of HRBP retained on RPs after the detergent wash could have interacted with LsCPT3 as a surrogate partner for its activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence identity data.

claim: No distinct interaction between LsCPT3 and HRBP can be detected by BiFC in the N. benthamiana system.
source: In practice, we have analysed cross-species interaction partnerships between cPT and NgBR family proteins from different plant species by BiFC in the N. benthamiana system, but no distinct interaction between LsCPT3 and HRBP can be detected (unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: The NgBR family protein may play an important role in proper introduction and folding of cPT or its stabilization on the ER membrane, especially in a heterologous cell expression system.
source: Taken together with the observation that distinct fluorescent signals for mTq2-fused HRT1 or HRT2 in N. benthamiana cells were detected only when they were co-expressed with mVanus-fused HRBP (Figure 5), the NgBR family protein may play an important role in proper introduction and folding of cPT or its stabilization on the ER membrane, especially in a heterologous cell expression system, which may be conserved in the RTase in NR-producing plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The absence of any RTase activity by HRT1 introduced on liposomes by the cell-free translation-coupled system suggests that structural arrangements of RPs and/or membrane proteins on RPs may be required for HRT1 to exhibit RTase activity.
source: The absence of any RTase activity by HRT1 introduced on liposomes by the cell-free translation-coupled system suggests that structural arrangements of RPs, a hydrophobic core of rubber molecules surrounded by a lipid monolayer, and/or membrane proteins on RPs may be required for HRT1 to exhibit RTase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative result with liposomes.

claim: Appropriate interactions between lipids and the proteins are required to facilitate accurate folding of membrane proteins during translation.
source: It has been demonstrated that appropriate interactions between lipids and the proteins are required to facilitate accurate folding of membrane proteins during translation (Cymer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Function and activity of membrane proteins depend critically on properties of the membrane applied, such as lipid composition, phase, tension, fluidity and curvature.
source: However, it has been pointed out that function and activity of the resulting proteins depend critically on properties of the membrane applied, such as lipid composition, phase, tension, fluidity and curvature (Cymer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Neither HRT1 nor HRT2 have any deduced transmembrane domains.
source: Although neither HRT1 nor HRT2 have any deduced transmembrane domains (predicted by TMHMM; http://www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/TMHMM/), these cPTs may require the membrane environment of RPs or the ER for accurate and functional folding, which is considered to correlate with incorporation of HRT1 into WRPs after cell-free synthesis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated based on computational prediction.

claim: HRT1 and HRT2 may require the membrane environment of RPs or the ER for accurate and functional folding.
source: Although neither HRT1 nor HRT2 have any deduced transmembrane domains (predicted by TMHMM; http://www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/TMHMM/), these cPTs may require the membrane environment of RPs or the ER for accurate and functional folding, which is considered to correlate with incorporation of HRT1 into WRPs after cell-free synthesis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The size distributions of rubber products from HRT1 and LsCPT3 were quite similar to each other.
source: Of note was that the size distributions of rubber products from HRT1 and LsCPT3 were quite similar to each other (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by GPC data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The molecular size of de novo synthesised rubber by recombinant cPTs may be determined not by catalytic properties of each cPT but by structural properties of RPs.
source: These results suggest that the molecular size of de novo synthesised rubber by recombinant cPTs may be determined not by catalytic properties of each cPT but by structural properties of RPs, although further investigations will be needed to elucidate the mechanism for chain-length determination of rubber products.
evidence: This is inferred from the GPC data.

claim: The architecture of RP is considered to be favourable for accommodation of extraordinarily long polyprenyl products formed by sequential condensation of IPP by an RP-localized RTase.
source: The architecture of RP is considered to be favourable for accommodation of extraordinarily long polyprenyl products formed by sequential condensation of IPP by an RP-localized RTase (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is stated as a consideration based on the structure of RPs.

claim: Srt1p was reported to be localized on lipid droplets in S. cerevisiae.
source: Srt1p was reported to be localized on lipid droplets in S. cerevisiae (Sato et al., 2001), and Nus1p was also detected on lipid droplets using a proteomic approach (Grillitsch et al., 2011), suggesting co-localization or interaction of these proteins on lipid droplets.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Nus1p was detected on lipid droplets using a proteomic approach.
source: Srt1p was reported to be localized on lipid droplets in S. cerevisiae (Sato et al., 2001), and Nus1p was also detected on lipid droplets using a proteomic approach (Grillitsch et al., 2011), suggesting co-localization or interaction of these proteins on lipid droplets.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: The fact that yeast does not show RTase activity suggests that arrangement of a cPT with an NgBR family protein on an organelle with a hydrophobic core to accommodate extraordinarily long polyprenyl products may not be a determinant for modification of the cPT into active RTase.
source: The fact that yeast does not show RTase activity suggests that arrangement of a cPT with an NgBR family protein on an organelle with a hydrophobic core to accommodate extraordinarily long polyprenyl products may not be a determinant for modification of the cPT into active RTase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that yeast does not produce rubber despite having similar organelles.

claim: HRT1 and HRT2 showed different subcellular localizations in the N. benthamiana expression system; HRT1 in the Golgi or ER and HRT2 on the plasma membrane.
source: In spite of high amino acid sequence identity between HRT1 and HRT2 (88%, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), these cPTs showed different subcellular localizations in the N. benthamiana expression system; HRT1 in the Golgi or ER and HRT2 on the plasma membrane (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cell biological roles of HRT2 in laticifer may be different from those of HRT1.
source: While subcellular localizations of HRT1 and HRBP are altered from the Golgi to the ER by co-expression of REF, HRT2 is translocated to the plasma membrane, accompanied by HRBP regardless of REF co-expression (Figure 5B), suggesting failure of REF to retain the HRT2-HRBP complex in the ER. These results suggest that cell biological roles of HRT2 in laticifer may be different from those of HRT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: This is the first report regarding the identification of a plasma membrane-localised eukaryotic cPT.
source: Cell biological roles of cPT on the plasma membrane remain to be elucidated and to the best of our knowledge, this is the first report regarding the identification of a plasma membrane-localised eukaryotic cPT.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding.

claim: HRT1 may be the principal catalytic component of RTase responsible for NR biosynthesis in H. brasiliensis.
source: In addition, HRT1 expression is severely restricted in the latex of H. brasiliensis, while HRT2 transcripts are detected in various tissues (Aoki et al., 2014a). According to the functional characterizations of HRT2 heterologously expressed in E. coli (Asawatreratanakul et al., 2003) and yeast (Takahashi et al., 2012), HRT2 essentially possess catalytic function as cPT or possibly as RTase. Nevertheless, above-mentioned evidences suggest a possibility that HRT1 may be the principal catalytic component of RTase responsible for NR biosynthesis in H. brasiliensis, although we still consider a possible involvement of other cPTs including HRT2 in the NR biosynthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns and functional characterizations.

claim: Two mechanisms for the NR biosynthesis have been proposed: de novo formation of NR via sequential cis-1,4-condensation of IPP onto short-chain allylic diphosphates as primer substrates, and elongation or addition of IPP at the α-terminal reactive moiety of pre-existing rubber molecules or polyprenyl diphosphates in RPs.
source: Two mechanisms for the NR biosynthesis have been proposed so far (Rojruthai et al., 2010): the first one is de novo formation of NR via sequential cis-1,4-condensation of IPP onto short-chain allylic diphosphates as primer substrates; the second one is elongation or addition of IPP at the α-terminal reactive moiety of pre-exiting rubber molecules or polyprenyl diphosphates in RPs.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: No detectable proteins responsible for the short-chain allylic diphosphate biosynthesis were found on the detergent-washed RPs.
source: The allylic diphosphate primer requirement for the RTase reaction (Figure 9C) and no detectable proteins responsible for the short-chain allylic diphosphate biosynthesis on the detergent-washed RPs (Figure 2—source data 1) suggest a possibility that HRT1 on WRP catalyzes a de novo rubber formation using allylic diphosphate as primer substrates.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: An alternative scenario is that HRT2 on the WRPs functions as cPT to form polyprenyl diphosphates, which might be utilised by HRT1 as acceptor substrates.
source: However, an alternative scenario that HRT2 on the WRPs functions as cPT to form polyprenyl diphosphates, which might be utilised by HRT1 as acceptor substrates in the latter NR biosynthetic mechanism, can not be ruled out.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis.

claim: HRBP is a distantly-related structural homolog of HRT1.
source: HRBP is a distantly-related structural homolog of HRT1. The amino acid sequence of HRBP shows some similarity to that of HRT1 (sequence identity: 10.9%), although only HRBP is predicted to have a membrane-spanning region at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: The amino acid sequence of HRBP shows some similarity to that of HRT1 (sequence identity: 10.9%).
source: HRBP is a distantly-related structural homolog of HRT1. The amino acid sequence of HRBP shows some similarity to that of HRT1 (sequence identity: 10.9%), although only HRBP is predicted to have a membrane-spanning region at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: HRT1 may form a heteromeric complex with HRBP rather than form a homomultimeric structure on RPs.
source: The results from the Y2H and BiFC assays show that HRBP interacts with HRT1, whereas HRT1 does not interact with itself; i.e., HRT1 may form a heteromeric complex with HRBP rather than form a homomultimeric structure on RPs, although HRBP also exhibited self-interaction in the Y2H and BiFC assays.
evidence: This is inferred from the Y2H and BiFC assay data.

claim: Reconstitution experiments with the two components on WRPs support the hypothesis that the reconstituted RTase activity is highest when HRT1 and HRBP are expressed at equivalent levels.
source: Reconstitution experiments with the two components on WRPs (Figure 9B) support this hypothesis: the reconstituted RTase activity is highest when these two components are expressed.
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: HRBP functions as a mediating protein between REF and HRT1 to form the ternary complex on RP.
source: Although we have no data for the stoichiometry of an HRBP-REF complex, specific interaction partnerships, HRT1-HRBP and HRBP-REF (Figures 3 and 4), and probable formation of the ternary complex (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) indicate that HRBP functions as a mediating protein between REF and HRT1 to form the ternary complex on RP.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Only when REF was co-expressed with HRT1 and HRBP, the reconstituted RTase activity showed a significant increase.
source: Additionally, only when REF was co-expressed with HRT1 and HRBP, the reconstituted RTase activity showed a significant increase.
evidence: This is supported by RTase activity assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The ternary complex including HRT1 may function as rubber-producing machinery on RPs.
source: Taken together, the ternary complex including HRT1 may function as rubber-producing machinery on RPs (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is inferred from the RTase activity assay data and interaction data.

claim: The amino acid sequence of SRPP contains a REF-homology domain.
source: Interestingly, the amino acid sequence of SRPP, another RP-abundant protein in H. brasiliensis, contains a REF-homology domain (Oh et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Several homologous proteins of SRPP have been identified not only from rubber-producing plants but also non-rubber producing plants, designated as the SRPP family or stress-related protein family.
source: To date, several homologous proteins of SRPP have been identified not only from rubber-producing plants but also non-rubber producing plants, designated as the SRPP family or stress-related protein family (Berthelot et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: No counterpart of REF, a shorter protein than SRPP family, has been found from other species.
source: However, no counterpart of REF, a shorter protein than SRPP family, has been found from other species.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on current knowledge.

claim: Silencing of a REF-related gene TbREF affected the rubber production in the RP of Russian dandelion.
source: Laibach et al. (2015) reported that silencing of a REF-related gene TbREF affected the rubber production in the RP of Russian dandelion, even though this gene is rather homologous to SRPP.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: REF modulates diameters of WRPs, representing the first direct evidence of REF being an important protein in the WRP stability.
source: Our observations of REF in modulating diameters of WRPs (Figure 8) represents the first direct evidence of REF being an important protein in the WRP stability.
evidence: This is supported by dynamic light scattering data shown in Figure 8.

claim: REF inserts into membranes and disrupts their integrity, whereas SRPP weakly interacts with membranes without any disruption.
source: Berthelot et al. (2014b) reported different behaviors of REF and SRPP on model membrane systems, where REF inserts into membranes and disrupts their integrity, whereas SRPP weakly interacts with membranes without any disruption.
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: REF is likely to insert itself into RP and is expected to interact with rubber molecules in RP.
source: Since REF is likely to insert itself into RP, it is expected to interact with rubber molecules in RP.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature about REF behavior on membranes.

claim: Similarities between the structures of RP and the ER-derived lipid droplet suggest that RPs may originate from the ER or Golgi apparatus.
source: Similarities between the structures of RP and the ER-derived lipid droplet (i.e. a hydrophobic core surrounded by a lipid monolayer) suggest that RPs may originate from the ER or Golgi apparatus (Chrispeels and Herman, 2000).
evidence: This is cited from literature.

claim: Various proteins homologous to vesicular trafficking-related proteins in the ER or Golgi apparatus were identified on WRPs.
source: This speculation was bolstered by identification of various proteins homologous to vesicular trafficking-related proteins in the ER or Golgi apparatus, on WRPs (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claim: The co-existence of marker proteins for other vesicles involved in different phases of membrane trafficking pathways on RPs suggests that RP formation and maturation may be complicated by fusion of multiple vesicles.
source: However, the co-existence of marker proteins for other vesicles involved in different phases of membrane trafficking pathways, e.g. the endocytic/endosomal compartments (RabA, RabC, RabE, RabF, an ArfB-type coat GTPase and clathrins), vacuoles (RabG) and lipid-bodies (β-1,3-glucase [Paul et al., 2014]), on RPs suggests that RP formation and maturation may be complicated by fusion of multiple vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data.

claim: Different subcellular localization of the protein complexes HRT1–HRBP and HRBP–REF may partly reflect the stepwise formation of the HRT1–HRBP–REF complex on RPs.
source: Different subcellular localization of the protein complexes HRT1–HRBP and HRBP–REF may partly reflect the stepwise formation of the HRT1–HRBP–REF complex on RPs (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data.

claim: Proteomics of the detergent-washed RPs did not identify any major lipid droplet proteins such as seipin, perilipins or oleosins.
source: In addition, proteomics of the detergent-washed RPs did not identify any major lipid droplet proteins such as seipin, perilipins or oleosins (Murphy, 2012), consistent with a previous proteomics study of RPs (Dai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data and cited literature.

claim: Mechanisms for de novo formation from the ER and maturation of RPs may be different from those of lipid droplets.
source: This implies that mechanisms for de novo formation from the ER and maturation of RPs may be different from those of lipid droplets.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data.

claim: This study represents important progress toward understanding the molecular machinery of rubber production on RP.
source: In conclusion, this study represents important progress toward understanding the molecular machinery of rubber production on RP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Identification of the two partner proteins of HRT1 provides suggestions for possible formation of a ternary complex that functions as the RTase.
source: Identification of the two partner proteins of HRT1 provides suggestions for possible formation of a ternary complex that functions as the RTase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: HRBP-REF interaction discovered in this study is specific to NR production.
source: Although the interactions between cPTs and NgBR homologs are generally assumed in other organisms, HRBP-REF interaction discovered in this study is specific to NR production.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Cell biological analyses of the localization of the three components suggest that RPs can be generated by a fusion of various cellular vesicles.
source: Cell biological analyses of the localization of the three components suggest that RPs can be generated by a fusion of various cellular vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: In vitro rubber production on WRP was demonstrated for the first time by heterologously expressing cPTs from the Para rubber tree and lettuce.
source: We demonstrated in vitro rubber production on WRP for the first time by heterologously expressing cPTs from the Para rubber tree and lettuce, although the assay system developed in this study still included a small amount of endogenous proteins sustained on WRPs.
